doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Father's advice to do it all; early jobs and the classical-jazz divide
summary: Music was the expected path. His father urged him to play every kind of music. Raph describes his early Broadway show, Sammy Kaye, opera and symphony work, and how classical players reacted to his jazz gigs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were your parents supportive of you going into music?

It was almost a gimme. It was just something to do. My father was in music, my mother didn’t much, she liked music and all, it was just the way to go. I took piano and when I was taking piano lessons at age eight, nine and ten I had visions of being a concert pianist. Music has always been kind of the goal. And my father did impress one thing on me which was really good and that is to do it all. To do as many different kinds of music as I could. So I made that a campaign. When I played trombone, and my first jobs on trombone I was lucky, I got a Broadway show almost right off the bat when I was twenty years old. After that I started paying dues. Because when the show closed I had nothing and I went out with Sammy Kaye on the road, I played with American Opera Society in New York City, I played a lot of subbing at the Radio City Music Hall, and doing shows and doing this kind of thing, plus playing the symphony against the popular or dance music end of it, kind of pointed me in the direction of being able to at least make contacts in the various fields of music. So on my dossier I write charter member of the American Symphony Orchestra with Leopold Stokowski, and at the same time I was a charter member of Gerry Mulligan’s concert jazz band. And in those days, while it wasn’t — it was rare, it wasn’t not heard of — but it was fairly rare to do both ends of the spectrum. I got a lot of raised eyebrows from various people along the way, until I finally realized that when I’m talking with jazz people I don’t talk classical, and when I’m talking with symphony people I don’t mention that I just did Birdland the night before.
They don’t feel that it’s really appropriate to be doing that?

At that time it was — what would I say — I won’t say threatening, that’s not a good word because I was too young in the stage of my career to be threatening to anybody. But when you’re talking, you know, back stage with a group of classical musicians, symphony musicians, the talk is about the symphony world and about the connections and the contractors and the opportunities and all of that. And then to pull in, well I played Birdland last night or I’ve been doing this, that and the other, it’s almost like stopping the conversation. Well okay, that’s nice, and what were we talking about now, you know.
